stories.summary: A high-stakes clash between global tech giants and national regulators has taken center stage over the future of satellite broadband in India. In this episode of Tech Today, Cyrus breaks down the regulatory standoff surrounding Starlink, takes a first look at Apple’s newly unveiled smart home hardware, and tests Xiaomi’s Mijia Smart Air Purifier 6 ahead of North India's winter pollution spike. The satellite internet debate escalated into a public spat after Elon Musk alleged that local business interests are obstructing Starlink’s rollout, prompting Indian authorities and Telecom Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia to firmly state that national security, data sovereignty, and regulatory frameworks apply equally to all operators. With India's satcom market projected to hit $14.8 billion by 2033, the struggle goes far beyond connecting remote regions; it is a battle over critical digital infrastructure, spectrum allocation, and stringent security mandates. We break down the government’s non-negotiable GMPCS requirements, including local gateway landing stations, strict real-time lawful interception, geographic beam kill-switches, and zero foreign data routing, alongside the economic challenge of high upfront dish costs versus low-cost Indian terrestrial 5G. In Tech & You, we look at Apple’s surprise smart home hardware announcements. Headlining the lineup is the Apple HomeView, a 7-inch wall- or table-mountable smart display priced at ₹39,900 that features Siri AI and recognizes up to six household members. Apple also introduced a refreshed Apple TV 4K at ₹39,900 with far-field voice microphones and Find My remote precision finding, the HomePod mini 2 at ₹18,900, and a broader connected home collection built with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. We evaluate whether Apple's premium pricing can successfully challenge established ecosystems like Amazon Alexa and Google Home. Finally, as seasonal AQI levels begin to rise across Delhi-NCR and the northern plains, we test the Xiaomi Mijia Smart Air Purifier 6, retailing at ₹19,999. Featuring five-stage filtration with primary, HEPA, activated carbon, UVC, and negative ion systems, the purifier is rated for up to 940 square feet with a 443 m³/h particle CADR. In our real-world candle smoke stress test, the unit reduced an extreme 600 AQI down to 54 within 35 minutes and reached 12 in about an hour. We review its compact build, quiet 32dB sleep mode, app controls, and how it compares to alternatives like the Honeywell Air Touch P2. Should national security guardrails take priority over rapid satellite internet rollouts, or is the process moving too slowly? Will Apple's premium HomeView smart display find a place in Indian living rooms? Drop your thoughts in the comments below! article_sentences: China on Monday said it would introduce export controls on tunnel-boring machines “to better safeguard national security and interests”, starting November 18.
India has already been facing difficulties in customs clearance and delays in importing TBMs from China for several critical infrastructure projects.

The latest announcement comes days after Beijing announced a plan to impose sweeping export controls on 40 cutting-edge technologies, including those for certain advanced solar manufacturing and some AI platforms.

The Chinese Commerce Ministry said on Monday in an announcement it was “introducing export controls on tunnel-boring machines and related items and optimising and adjusting export-control measures for certain dredgers and related items.” The measures will take effect on November 18.

The ministry said prior to the announcement, China had “notified the relevant countries and regions with which it has established export-control dialogue mechanisms.” “The items covered by these measures have clear dual-use (civilian and military) characteristics,” the announcement said.

“The measures are intended to better safeguard national security and interests, while also enabling China to better fulfil its international obligations, including those related to non-proliferation”.

India has previously raised with China the delays in customs clearance for imports of TBMs, which are used in India for several critical projects including the construction of metro rail networks in cities, railway corridors and key tunnelling projects, including in border areas.
India is dependent on imports for the machines.
Difficulties in imports from China started in 2024.

In October of that year, Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal had publicly raised the issue with visiting German Vice Chancellor Robert Habeck, pointing out that China was blocking the export of TBMs made by a German company in China.
On Monday, China also announced export control measures related to certain types of drones.

The controlled items include ”autopilots specially designed for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs); UAVs or unmanned airships with a maximum endurance of three hours or more; certain engines specially designed for UAVs or unmanned airships; and UAVs with a range of 300 kilometers or more”, among other items.

stories.title: Karnataka High Court Grants Bail To Pan Masala Manufacturer In Rs. 42 Crore Health Security & National Security Cess Evasion Case

article_sentences: The Karnataka High Court has recently granted bail to S. Nithyananda-the proprietor of M/s N Square Enterprises-who was arrested under the newly enacted Health Security and National Security Cess (HSNS) Act, 202 for allegedly evading cess amounting to around 42 crores.
The single judge bench of Justice S Vishwajith Shetty granted him bail on October 17[Saturday].

The accused had been in judicial custody since August 20, 2026, following a crackdown by the Directorate General of GST Intelligence (DGGI), Bengaluru Zonal Unit at his factory in Nelamangala, and his residence in Sheshadripuram.

According to DGGI, the search of the factory led to the recovery of six undeclared vertical Forms, Fill and Seal (FFS) pouch packing machines, alongside large quantities of raw materials, packaging materials, and finished pan masala goods.

The department had earlier alleged that the accused was engaged in unregulated manufacture and clearance of pan masala, without following the norms for registration, declaration of machinery, or payment of applicable cess.
After the search, the DGGI computed the alleged evasion around Rs 1 crore per machine every month, with a total liability of around 42 crores for the time period of February 2026 -August 2026.

After his arrest, Nityananda had filed bail applications which were previously rejected by the Special Court for Economic Offences on September 1, and thereafter, the Sessions Court on October 6, 2026.
Senior Advocate Sunil Kumar S., appearing for the petitioner, argued that the entire case rests on a presumptive calculation of cess.
He heavily relied on the recent judgment of the High Court of Karnataka in M/s Dhariwal Industries Pvt.
Union of India, wherein a Single Judge bench of Justice M Nagaprasanna struck down the capacity-based manner of levying cess under the HSNS Act as violative of Article 14.
Though the Division Bench then subsequently stayed the single bench order, the petitioner contended that the liability to the tune of 42 crores attributed is a disputed departmental calculation.
Kumar argued that it should not be treated as a final adjudicated liability at the bail stage.

stories.headline: Unleashing India's potential over 25 years
stories.title: Unleashing India's potential over 25 years
stories.summary: On October 7, 2001, Narendra Modi took oath as chief minister of Gujarat. Twenty-five years later, that milestone offers an opportunity to reflect not only on a quarter century of public service, but also on how profoundly India itself has changed during the same period.I have had the privilege of witnessing this transformation through the lens of business. The Mahindra Group has businesses across 20 industries that comprise nearly 70 percent of India’s GDP, including agriculture, mobility, technology, financial services, aerospace, logistics, real estate and hospitality. Across these sectors, one change has been unmistakable: The scale of the India opportunity has expanded dramatically.In 2001, India had enormous potential, but that potential was constrained by gaps in infrastructure, connectivity, technology and access. Today, India is a far more connected, capable and globally consequential economy.The numbers tell part of the story. India’s economy was around $500 billion in 2001; by 2026, it is close to $4 trillion. But GDP alone cannot capture the transformation. The more interesting story is how opportunity has increasingly moved from being concentrated in a few places and institutions to becoming accessible to millions more.Connectivity to opportunityConsider how an Indian citizen interacts with the economy today.A small entrepreneur can receive a payment instantly from a customer thousands of kilometres away. A farmer can access information through a mobile phone. A young person in a small town can build a business for a global market. A consumer can access financial services without necessarily stepping into a bank branch.Digital public infrastructure has changed the architecture of opportunity. Aadhaar, Jan Dhan and UPI have helped deepen financial inclusion and formalisation, while UPI has demonstrated how technology, scale and inclusion can work together.This is not simply a technology story. It is an India story: The movement from access being a privilege to access becoming increasingly ubiquitous.Also Read: 25 years of Prime Minister Narendra Modi in public office: Shaping governanceFrom infrastructure deficit to a new realityThe physical transformation has been equally significant.India has expanded its highways, airports, ports, metro systems, rail networks and digital connectivity at a scale that would have been difficult to imagine two decades ago. We are adding an airport a month for the past few years, and more than 30 to 34 km of roads daily, nearly three times the pace a decade ago. Electricity access, too, has expanded dramatically, with World Bank data showing 99.5 percent access in 2023.Infrastructure is not an end in itself. It is an enabler. Better connectivity allows a manufacturer to source more efficiently, a farmer to reach markets faster, a tourist to travel more easily and a young person to access opportunities beyond the geography in which they were born.What I saw from the industry sideMy year as President of FICCI gave me another perspective on this transformation.We worked with more than 500 CEOs and 30 ministries on more than 100 initiatives spanning Make in India, women-led development, farm prosperity and sustainability. I personally participated in more than 200 meetings with senior government leaders and saw first-hand how industry and government could engage on complex economic and policy questions.What stayed with me was the willingness to listen.Industry would bring specific recommendations, sometimes involving difficult policy choices. The response was often to engage with the substance: To ask questions,challenge assumptions and explore what could be done.Constructive dialogue matters. Government brings the policy framework and public-interest perspective; industry brings ground-level experience, investment and execution capability. When the two engage seriously, the potential for outcomes that benefit both the economy and businesses increases.I believe this partnership will be particularly important in India’s next phase of growth.Potential to executionPerhaps the most important change has been India’s growing confidence in executing at scale.Over the past decade, the country has undertaken large national programmes across financial inclusion, sanitation, housing, renewable energy, digital infrastructure and manufacturing. The pandemic provided a particularly powerful demonstration of India’s ability to coordinate institutions, technology, manufacturing and public systems at enormous scale.For business, this creates a new opportunity. India is no longer only a large market to serve. It can increasingly be a place from which to build products, technologies and businesses for the world.Manufacturing will be central to this next chapter.The global reconfiguration of supply chains presents India with an important opportunity. Initiatives such as the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes have sought to attract investment, deepen domestic capabilities and integrate Indian manufacturers more closely with global value chains. As of December 2025, the schemes had attracted more than ₹2.16 lakh crore of investment and generated over ₹20 lakh crore in production and sales across 14 sectors.But opportunity is not automatic. Productivity, skills, logistics, ease of doing business and supply-chain competitiveness will determine how far India can go.At the Mahindra Group, we see this every day—in automobiles, tractors, electric mobility, aerospace and advanced technology. The aspiration should be straightforward: Make world-class products in India, innovate in India and compete with the world.The next frontier is peopleThe next 25 years will require a different kind of transformation.India’s greatest asset is its people. Our demographic dividend will become an economic dividend only if young Indians have the education, skills and opportunities required for the jobs of the future.We must focus on skilling youth for industry readiness with industry as an active participant.We must also unlock the enormous potential of women in the workforce. Greater participation is not only a question of equity; it is an economic imperative. A country of India’s scale cannot realise its full potential if a significant part of its talent remains under-utilised.Businesses, therefore, have a responsibility beyond creating jobs. We must build skills, encourage entrepreneurship and create pathways for more people to participate meaningfully in the formal economy.Growth must also become increasingly sustainable. Climate change, energy transition, resource security and urbanisation will shape the competitiveness of both nations and companies. Long-term value creation will need to consider financial performance alongside the impact on people, communities and the environment.From potential to prosperityPerhaps the greatest transformation is intangible.In 2001, India was often described through the lens of what it could become. Today, the conversation increasingly centres on what India can build, lead, and contribute to the world.Indian entrepreneurs are building global companies. Indian technology is reaching international markets. Indian manufacturing is becoming part of global supply chains. Indian innovations in digital payments, healthcare and space are attracting global attention.Yet confidence must be accompanied by humility. India still has significant challenges—from inequality and skills to urbanisation, agricultural productivity, and the creation of quality employment.Twenty-five years of public service, therefore, provides an opportunity not simply to look back, but to ask what comes next.The India of 2001 had aspiration. The India of 2026 has demonstrated growing capability. The India of 2047 must translate that capability into broad-based, sustainable and enduring prosperity.That is the next chapter of the India story and one that all of us have a role in writing.

For business, this creates a new opportunity.
India is no longer only a large market to serve.
It can increasingly be a place from which to build products, technologies and businesses for the world.
Manufacturing will be central to this next chapter.
The global reconfiguration of supply chains presents India with an important opportunity.

Initiatives such as the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes have sought to attract investment, deepen domestic capabilities and integrate Indian manufacturers more closely with global value chains.
As of December 2025, the schemes had attracted more than ₹2.16 lakh crore of investment and generated over ₹20 lakh crore in production and sales across 14 sectors.

Productivity, skills, logistics, ease of doing business and supply-chain competitiveness will determine how far India can go.
At the Mahindra Group, we see this every day—in automobiles, tractors, electric mobility, aerospace and advanced technology.

stories.headline: 25 years of Prime Minister Narendra Modi in public office: Shaping governance
stories.title: 25 years of Prime Minister Narendra Modi in public office: Shaping governance
stories.summary: Any person, place, organisation or nation would change with time. If the period is 25 years, these changes can be expected to be deeper, wider, profound and fundamental.None of this commonsense anticipation could have prepared India and the world for the distance the country has traversed since Narendra Modi assumed public office for the first time—on October 7, 2001—as Gujarat’s chief minister. To put these momentous changes in perspective and construe what they augur for the future, we sought out some of the best and brightest minds, a select group that has been in the thick of things one way or the other.What emerges is that India has indeed transformed its economy, infrastructure, digital architecture, foreign policy, workforce, tax laws, energy mix, space programme, treatment of companies, approach to investors, and many other areas that influence the economy and industry, as well as human life in general. But there is another change—more subtle but just as impactful, perhaps more. Which is the way Indians, filled with never-seen-before self-assurance and ambition, view themselves and their place in the world.Anish Shah, group CEO of Mahindra Group, says in his article that the numbers tell only part of the story. Sure, it is nothing short of stupendous that India’s economy has grown from $500 billion in 2001 to nearly $4 trillion. But the more interesting story is “how opportunity has increasingly moved from being concentrated in a few places and institutions to becoming accessible to millions more”.Also Read: Unleashing India's potential over 25 yearsAshishkumar Chauhan, writing for us while still emerging from the demanding process of orchestrating one of the largest IPOs in India’s capital markets history, points out that when Modi took charge as Gujarat’s chief minister for the first time, the state was still reeling from the Kutch earthquake of January that year. “He did not inherit a growth story; he had to build one,” says the CEO of the National Stock Exchange of India.What a story it turned out to be! That combination of infrastructure first, direct investor engagement and follow-through became the template later scaled nationally. Modi’s stated philosophy, Chauhan says, is together with all, development for all, trust of all, and effort of all. “In capital markets, at least,” he says, “that has taken a concrete form: The growth of Indian enterprise is increasingly being funded by Indian savers.”Arundhati Bhattacharya, CEO of Salesforce South Asia, sees it as the story of how a country once defined by scarcity, distance and administrative complexity began using technology to turn scale into economic strength. What emerges is that India has indeed transformed its economy, infrastructure, digital architecture, foreign policy, workforce, tax laws, energy mix, space programme, treatment of companies, approach to investors, and many other areas that influence the economy and industry, as well as human life in general.
But there is another change—more subtle but just as impactful, perhaps more.
Which is the way Indians, filled with never-seen-before self-assurance and ambition, view themselves and their place in the world.
Anish Shah, group CEO of Mahindra Group, says in his article that the numbers tell only part of the story.

stories.title: COVER STORY: India's Solar Opportunities & The Challenges Ahead
stories.summary: 01 / THE BOTTLENECK What Are The Key Challenges In India’s Solar Market? Most seasoned industry leaders said that while India is making progressive strides towards adopting solar power, several bottlenecks continue to hinder its growth. Going forward, the biggest challenge will be to integrate growing solar into the grid, and to match it with demand profiles, which peaks during non-solar hours. This will require extensive planning, significant investment in expanding and modernizing grid infrastructure, and in supporting growth of energy storage to enable “peak shifting”. So, between now and 2030, we think the challenge is less about adding more gigawatts, and more about grid integration. Srivatsan Iyer, Global CEO, Hero Future Energies ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- As solar penetration rises, the challenge is that incremental generation is concentrated in the same daylight hours. The issue therefore shifts from the cost of producing a unit of solar electricity to its value to the grid at the time it is produced. We have already seen this globally through curtailment, low or even negative prices during high renewable hours and increasing evening flexibility requirements and these scenarios are emerging in India too. Deepak Thakur, MD & CEO, Hinduja Renewables ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- India’s renewable-energy sector is entering a period of very strong growth and is among the most remarkable story globally. Demand is expanding rapidly, particularly from commercial and industrial customers and from new areas such as data centres and AI infrastructure. The opportunity for solar and hybrid renewable energy is therefore very significant. The next phase will be about managing that growth effectively – ensuring that generation, infrastructure, technology and storage evolve together with rising demand. Kuldeep Jain, Founder & MD, Cleanmax ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Module capacity has moved well ahead of cell capacity, and cells are well ahead of wafers and ingots, which are still largely imported. As ALMM List-II for cells comes into effect, with a limited transition window for certain projects, the real test is whether domestic cell capacity can keep pace with module demand. A sector that assembles at home but depends on others for its core components has not yet secured its energy sovereignty. Closing that gap, cells first and then wafers and ingots, is the biggest task between now and 2030. Sohan Lal Agarwal, CMD, Websol Energy System Limited ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- In some regions, renewable capacity is growing faster than transmission and evacuation infrastructure, leading to grid congestion, curtailment and project delays. Ensuring that transmission and grid infrastructure keeps pace with generation will therefore be critical to fully utilising the renewable capacity India is adding. The biggest challenge will be moving from adding solar capacity to integrating it. Rupul Gupta, Founder, MD and CEO, TrueRE Orion Power ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Transmission delays, curtailment risks in resource-rich states and the gap between when the sun shines and when India actually needs power are the real constraints. Closely tied to this is the financial health of distribution companies. Developers can only scale with confidence if offtake is reliable and payments are timely. And we cannot ignore supply-chain dependence. Reducing reliance on imported cells, wafers and polysilicon is essential for long-term resilience. Harsan Patel, Whole Time Director, KPI Green Energy 02 / THE STORAGE QUESTION Solar and storage: how soon is the marriage inevitable? There is an agreement that storage will play an important role. Speakers highlighted that solar power and BESS are gradually becoming inseparable, with their integration expected to become more prominent. When we began building solar plants, the conversation was only about megawatts and tariffs. Today, every serious discussion we have with a DISCOM or a large customer comes back to one question: Can you give us power when we actually need it? Solar alone cannot answer that question. Solar with storage can. We see this in our own portfolio. Just a few years ago, storage was treated as an experiment. Today it is part of the project everyone asks about first. Venugopal Rao Maddireddy, CMD, Pace Digitek Ltd ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Rooftop solar and batteries are expected to converge in India over the next decade, shifting from an optional add-on to a standard configuration, led by commercial and industrial consumers. There are several reasons why the rooftop solar plus storage market is poised to grow. Time-of-day tariffs, which have been introduced for a larger number of consumers in several states, change more during peak hours of electricity use, such as the evening. Pawan Garg, CMD, Fujiyama ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- As solar penetration rises, managing intermittency, transmission, land, curtailment and evening peak demand will become increasingly important. India’s electricity demand is also rising at night, particularly due to cooling, while solar generation falls after sunset. The sector therefore needs to focus not just on adding GW, but on evacuation infrastructure, storage, forecasting and system flexibility. Gautam Mohanka, Director, Gautam Solar ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Every new solar tender now carries a minimum two-hour storage requirement at 10% of capacity. SECI’s latest FDRE tender is 1,200 MW with 4,800 MWh BESS attached. Such bids will be standard practice now. That demand pulls storage, and storage pulls everything else. The next phase of solar growth will be decided by who is buying, not by what we are building. Without grid expansion and large-scale BESS, we are forcing assets to sit idle and bleed revenue. Sanjeev Agarwal, Founder and Chairman, Hexa Climate ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The market is shifting from simply buying low-cost renewable power to asking for firm, peak-hour and more reliable supply. That naturally increases the role of storage. For commercial and industrial users, adoption will depend on battery costs, tariff structures and the value of backup and peak-demand management. Residential adoption is likely to be more selective for some time, depending on local economics and reliability needs. Ishver Dholakia, Founder & MD, Goldi Solar ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The CEA has proposed that new ground-mounted solar and wind projects commissioned after July 2027 include co-located storage. Firm-power tenders already demand four hours of storage. The bigger change is in what the industry sells. The unit of value is moving from megawatts of capacity installed to megawatt-hours delivered on demand. Winners will be those who can design, integrate and guarantee dispatch, not just those who install panels at the lowest cost. Raju Komaravolu, CEO, Energy & Capital Goods (India), Zetwerk ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- As solar penetration increases, four things will decide success: strengthening transmission and power evacuation, adding battery storage and forecasting for grid flexibility, speeding up land acquisition and connectivity approvals, and reducing financing costs and regulatory uncertainty. We also need deeper domestic manufacturing beyond module assembly for long-term energy security. Col Pravir Mishra, COO, Insolare Energy Limited ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- With domestic cell requirements taking effect from June 2026, strengthening the upstream ecosystem is critical. Wafers and ingots still remain largely import-dependent, underlining the need to deepen domestic manufacturing across the value chain. The second challenge is transmission, taking operational capacity to approximately 8.5 GW, while solar-plus-four-hour-storage tariffs have fallen to ₹2.70–2.76 per kWh. Policy support through viability-gap funding is also helping accelerate adoption. Ankit Singhania, Director, Navitas Solar 03 / THE GROWTH DRIVER What are the next big drivers of solar growth? Industry leaders also shared their views on the potential drivers of growth in India’s solar market. These included agrivoltaics, floating solar, and other emerging solar applications. Beyond conventional utility-scale and rooftop solar, major growth drivers for India include solar-plus-storage, data-centre power demand in the commercial and industrial segment, and new applications such as floating solar and agrivoltaics. Green hydrogen also has significant long-term potential, particularly for industries such as steel, refining and fertilisers, but its growth will depend on achieving commercially viable production costs. Harendra Tomar, Leader – Business Development, Sungrow ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- As solar penetration increases, the industry will also have to address land availability, project execution, financing and regulatory timelines more efficiently. These are not challenges for developers alone; they require coordination across the entire energy ecosystem. I believe the period to 2030 will mark a shift from capacity-led growth to system-led growth. The winners of the next phase will be those who can look beyond the solar plant itself and understand the complete journey of power—from generation to transmission, storage and consumption. Ravi Patel, Director – Sales & Marketing, Knack Energy ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- India’s next phase of solar growth will be shaped by emerging technologies such as floating solar, agrivoltaics and green hydrogen, supported by battery energy storage systems (BESS) and grid modernisation. Generating more solar power is only part of the story. The larger task is making that power reliable, flexible and available when it is needed. We see agrivoltaics as a promising way to expand solar capacity. Simarpreet Singh, Executive Director and CEO, Hartek Power ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- One of the key constraints today is the availability of suitable land and adequate evacuation infrastructure for large-scale projects. In this context, alternative models such as floating solar and agrivoltaics are poised to gain traction in the near term. Among these, agrivoltaics holds particular promise, as it enables dual use of land—supporting both agriculture and energy generation. With the right policy incentives and regulatory support, agrivoltaics could emerge as a highly efficient and scalable solution for India’s next phase of solar growth. Tanmoy Duari, Axitec Energy India Pvt. Limited ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- India has 140M farmers. Agrivoltaics (solar + farming on same land) solves land conflict. PM KUSUM already is targeting 34 GW. With elevated structures, farmer earns Rs 40k/acre from solar + crop income. This is bankable because farmer gets dual income, and you get land without acquisition headache. Gujarat & Maharashtra are already financing at scale. India has 18,000 sq km of reservoirs. No land cost, 10% higher yield due to cooling are added benefits. Vikass Agarwwal, Founder & CEO, DebtBridge ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- We see the next growth coming from solar that fits into everyday life and from new applications creating demand for clean electricity. Distributed solar added about 16.3 GW in FY26, over a third of the year's additions. Floating solar is a good example of thinking ahead. India has only about 700 MW today, against a NISE potential of around 102 GW. The new PM Surya Sarovar Yojana backs 5,000 MW with 10,000 MWh of storage, and it uses water bodies instead of competing for land. Rajesh Kaushal, EIS Business Group Head (India & SAARC), Delta Electronics India ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- So far, lower power cost was the driver but from here on, decarbonization, green economy and net zero will be the bigger drivers of Solar energy growth in next decade. The government has mandated that minimum 10% of the storage is required so definitely storage and Solar will go together. Eventually if we consider NET ZERO targets we need to store maximum solar energy into the battery and use them during non-solar hour. Bharat Chhittarkka, Managing Director, Trex Energy ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The one thing people underestimate is commercial and industrial demand. Green open access rules have been eased, and companies now have R100 targets and export customers to answer to, especially with CBAM in force in Europe. Clean power is becoming a procurement requirement for Indian industry, not a CSR line. On the residential side, PM Surya Ghar has taken rooftop solar into tier-2 and tier-3 towns. Together, distributed solar is turning into a large market in its own right. Deepak Jain, CTO, INA Solar ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Green hydrogen, floating solar and agrivoltaics each have strong potential. Green hydrogen can help industries cut emissions. Floating solar makes use of water bodies, and agrivoltaics allows farming and power generation on the same land. What they share is that they all extend solar beyond the traditional rooftop and ground-mounted plant. We believe the next phase of growth will come from solar combined with storage and tailored to specific needs, such as industrial power, land-constrained areas and farming communities. How fast each one grows will depend on falling costs, supportive policy and successful pilot projects. Sunsure Energy 04 / A SNEAK PEEK INTO THE FUTURE Where is the solar market heading to? Several industry leaders also offered a glimpse into the future of India’s solar market, drawing on past learnings, evolving policies, emerging trends, and other key developments shaping the sector. More tenders now require solar with storage, round-the-clock supply or firm power. What we’re still waiting for is the economics and the market rules to catch up so this can accelerate. The government is helping. Phase III of the Green Energy Corridor has just been approved, at Rs 1.86 lakh crore, and it should help move up to 135 GW of renewable power and add 50 GWh of battery storage. Srivatsan Iyer, Global CEO, Hero Future Energies ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Standalone solar will continue to make economic sense where daytime demand exists or the grid can absorb the generation. But as more solar enters the same daytime window, simply adding generation does not solve the larger power system requirement. The next unit of renewable capacity increasingly must solve for when power is required, not merely how much can be generated. Deepak Thakur, MD & CEO, Hinduja Renewables ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- In my view, storage becomes inseparable from utility-scale solar by regulation around 2027–28, and from C&I solar by economics in the states that move first. The bigger change is in what the industry sells. The unit of value is moving from megawatts of capacity installed to megawatt-hours delivered on demand. Winners will be those who can design, integrate and guarantee dispatch, not just those who install panels at the lowest cost. Raju Komaravolu, CEO, Energy & Capital Goods (India), Zetwerk ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- By 2030, I do not expect storage to be standard across every solar project. However, I do expect it to become a much more important part of how solar is planned and valued, especially since a significant amount of energy generated today is going unused or being wasted. The conversation will gradually shift from how cheaply solar can generate power to when that power can be delivered and how reliably it can meet demand. Ishver Dholakia, MD, Goldi Solar ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The economics have also turned decisively. When Madhya Pradesh can secure solar-plus-storage power at a record-low Rs 2.70 per unit, the argument that storage is too expensive is simply over. Regulators have noticed too. Maharashtra now requires battery storage with new rooftop solar above 100 kW, and we expect other states to follow sooner than people think. Venugopal Rao Maddireddy, CMD, Pace Digitek Ltd ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Beyond generation, the convergence of solar with green hydrogen, green ammonia, data centres and other energy-intensive applications is creating entirely new consumption models. This broader convergence is reflected in our SCALE strategy, where we are leveraging technology, AI and partnerships and expanding into emerging clean-energy applications and new forms of energy consumption. Rupul Gupta, Founder, MD & CEO, TrueRE Orion Power ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Buyers want reliable, round-the-clock supply, and the best answer will vary by region, resource and load profile. Wind-solar hybrid, and batteries will each have a role, and many projects will combine them. We serve round-the-clock needs today through wind-solar hybrid solutions, which complement storage. We expect this integrated approach to become the norm for new large-scale and commercial and industrial projects over the next four to five years. Kuldeep Jain, Founder and MD, CleanMax ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- But the real driver is on the demand side, not the supply side. Data centres. Companies like Google, Microsoft and Amazon are buying firm clean power at a scale that changes what we build, and they will not sign a contract that looks green on paper while drawing coal after sunset. That demand pulls storage, and storage pulls everything else. The next phase of solar growth will be decided by who is buying, not by what we are building. Sanjeev Agarwal, Founder and Chairman, Hexa Climate

The larger task is making that power reliable, flexible and available when it is needed.
We see agrivoltaics as a promising way to expand solar capacity.

Agrivoltaics (solar + farming on same land) solves land conflict.
PM KUSUM already is targeting 34 GW.

This is bankable because farmer gets dual income, and you get land without acquisition headache.
Gujarat & Maharashtra are already financing at scale.
India has 18,000 sq km of reservoirs.
No land cost, 10% higher yield due to cooling are added benefits.

This broader convergence is reflected in our SCALE strategy, where we are leveraging technology, AI and partnerships and expanding into emerging clean-energy applications and new forms of energy consumption.

Wind-solar hybrid, and batteries will each have a role, and many projects will combine them.
We serve round-the-clock needs today through wind-solar hybrid solutions, which complement storage.
We expect this integrated approach to become the norm for new large-scale and commercial and industrial projects over the next four to five years.

Data centres.

Companies like Google, Microsoft and Amazon are buying firm clean power at a scale that changes what we build, and they will not sign a contract that looks green on paper while drawing coal after sunset.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court has stayed the execution of the death sentence handed down to an Indian Mujahideen operative for his role in the 2008 Ahmedabad serial bomb blasts that left 56 people dead.
A bench of Justices Vikram Nath, Sandeep Mehta and Aparesh Kumar Singh agreed to hear a plea filed by convict Mohammad Tanvir, who has challenged the Gujarat High Court's July 7 verdict.
On July 7, the high court upheld the death sentences of 38 operatives of terror outfit Indian Mujahideen in the serial-bomb-blasts case.
The High Court had cited the large number of casualties, the "humongous" nature of the conspiracy and the intention to spread widespread terror as key reasons for affirming the punishment.
On July 26, 2008, a series of 21 bomb blasts ripped through different areas of Ahmedabad in a span of 70 minutes, killing 56 people and leaving more than 200 injured.
"There shall be stay of execution of the death sentence awarded to the appellant (Tanvir)," the top court said in its October 9 order.
It said the original records of the case be summoned from the Trial Court and the High Court.
The apex court asked the Gujarat government to place the reports of all probation officers relating to the appellant before it within eight weeks.

It directed the superintendent of the jail concerned to submit a report with regard to the nature of work that has been performed by the appellant while in prison and also regarding his conduct and behaviour within eight weeks.

"The superintendent of prison of the concerned prison shall also get done the psychological evaluation of the appellant from the government medical hospital," the bench said, adding that a report of the evaluation be submitted to the court within eight weeks.
It posted the matter for hearing after 12 weeks.
On October 1, the apex court stayed the execution of the death penalty of Ahmed Bawa alias Abbu Abubakar Barelvi, one of the convicts in the case.

stories.title: India-New Zealand FTA: Comm Min notifies tariff rate quota for apples, kiwifruit, Manuka honey
stories.summary: India is allowing specified quantities of these products to enter at concessional import duty rates under the pact
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: With the India-New Zealand free trade agreement set to be effective on October 20, the Commerce Ministry on Monday laid out a procedure to allocate concessional duty-based quotas for imports of apples, kiwifruit, and Manuka honey from the island nation.

Under the pact, India is providing Tariff Rate Quotas (TRQs) in a calibrated manner for apples, kiwifruit, Manuka Honey and Albumins, along with Minimum Import Price (MIP) provisions and other safeguard measures.
This approach ensures calibrated imports while protecting the domestic farmers' interests.
"The procedure for allocation of TRQ under the India- New Zealand Free Trade Agreement is notified," the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) said in a public notice.
India is allowing specified quantities of these products to enter at concessional import duty rates under the pact.
According to the notice, these provisions will take effect on October 20, 2026.
For apples, there will be no quota in the first year.
The quota will be 35,000 tonnes in the second year, rising to 37,500 tonnes in the third, 40,000 tonnes in the fourth and 42,500 tonnes in the fifth.
From the sixth year onwards, it will be 45,000 tonnes a year.
These imports will attract a 25 per cent duty, provided their cost, insurance and freight (CIF) value is at least USD 1.25 per kg.
The annual import window will run from April 1 to August 31.
At present, India has a 50 per cent import duty on apples.

stories.headline: Innovations are bringing in new ways to manage diabetes
stories.title: Innovations are bringing in new ways to manage diabetes
stories.summary: According to a study published in The Lancet Diabetes and Endocrinology journal, India is home to 90 million people living with diabetes, as of 2024 (the most recent year of study), and ranks second in the world, second to China, with 148 million diabetics. The rising number of diabetics in India makes the country an attractive market for pharmaceutical companies, whether Indian or foreign. According to the National Family Health Survey-6 (NFHS-6), published in May, 17.8 percent of women in India are now on diabetes medication compared to 13.5 percent in 2021 (NFHS-5), while the numbers jumped from 15.6 percent to 20.9 percent for men.Keeping pace with the rising number of diabetics has been the number of innovations in the formulations and delivery mechanisms of diabetes medication. The most recent and significant developments have been the wider availability of semaglutide medications—after the patent for semaglutide drugs expired in March 2026, the prices of generic semaglutide have reduced significantly—and insulin doses that can be taken less frequently and more easily than before. There has also been an underlying shift in the approach to diabetes treatment: Instead of treating the condition in isolation of other health conditions such as heart diseases, high blood pressure and morbidity, it is now increasingly treated as part of a cohesive whole, along with other medical conditions.New drugs and deliveriesThis July, Danish drugmaker Novo Nordisk introduced its once-a-week insulin Awiqly in India, the seventh market to have the product. The company describes Awiqly as the world's first once-weekly basal, or background long-acting, insulin for of type 1 and type 2 diabetes in adults. It is designed to reduce the number of injections from 365 per year (for diabetics who need to take one insulin injection every day) to 52, and costs about Rs 2,611 for a 700-unit pen, averaging around Rs 261 per week. Daily insulin injections cost patients about Rs 300 per week.Dr Pranav Ghody, consultant endocrinologist and diabetologist, Wockhardt Hospitals, Mumbai, says the research around insulins at the beginning of the century started with scientists trying to engineer an insulin similar to human insulin. “Previous generations of insulins were engineered to overcome one of the shortcomings of the first basal insulins, which was not lasting a full 24 hours. Awiqli has been engineered on the same platform by substituting three amino acids in the protein sequence and adding an ultra-long fatty side chain of a human insulin which binds to the protein albumin, making it last much longer,” he explains.Vikrant Shrotriya, managing director of Novo Nordisk India, says insulin is still considered a sign of morbidity among a lot of people. “It’s a psycho-social issue. There is a lot of inertia, and a lot of taboos among people. It requires a lot of counselling.”Dr Manoj Chawla, diabetologist at Mumbai’s Hinduja Hospital, says a weekly dosage will ensure easier acceptance among patients who are starting to take insulin. “The number of injections go down from 365 to 52 in a year, and hence makes initiation of insulin more acceptable,” he says. “What it does not do is replace the mealtime insulin, which is mandatory for type 1 diabetes. Some people with type 2 diabetes who also use the mealtime insulin will have to continue doing so.”Another significant development that has impacted the diabetes medication ecosystem is the expiration of patents on semaglutide drugs. The advent of GLP-1 (glucagone-like peptide) drugs such as semaglutide, tirzepatide, dulaglutide in 2005 changed the way diabetes began to be treated across the globe.At the turn of the century, managing diabetes was about taking medication that stabilised blood glucose levels, says Dr Hema Venkataraman, lead consultant, endocrinology, KIMS Hospitals, Bengaluru. “Metformin, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones, and insulin dominated the practice, while cardiovascular diseases, kidney disease, and obesity were managed as separate problems,” she says. “Today’s standards of care tell a different story. Treatment is now individualised around cardiovascular risk, kidney disease, obesity, hypoglycaemia, diabetes technology, and patient preferences.”“GLP-1 receptor agonists and newer dual incretin therapies improve insulin secretion, suppresses glucagon, slows gastric emptying and reduces appetite. In people with diabetes, they improve glycaemic control while also producing weight loss. In people with obesity, they are prescribed primarily to achieve weight reduction, often at different doses. The important point is that we are increasingly treating metabolic disease rather than isolated diseases like diabetes or obesity. The choice of therapy depends on the patient's overall clinical profile, cardiovascular risk, kidney function, body weight and treatment goals,” Venkataraman explains.GLP-1 treatment itself has also evolved over the years. Earlier, GLP agonist (byetta) had to be injected twice a day, then came a daily GLP agonist called Liraglutide and Victoza, and now semaglutides are a version with an extended half-life of the molecule. This has been achieved by adding a fatty acid side chain so that it binds to albumin, which makes it last much longer within the body.With the expiration of patents this March, the prices of generic semaglutide drugs have fallen to Rs 1,290 to Rs 1,800 per month, making them more accessible and affordable. Patented semaglutide drugs such as Ozempic (by Novo Nordisk) cost Rs 5,660 to Rs 9,000 per month, while Mounjaro (by Eli Lilly) start at Rs 13,125 and could go up to Rs 25,781 per month. The monthly cost for metformin is between Rs 20 and Rs 300, depending on generic or branded variants, while for sulfonylureas it is Rs 190 to Rs 3,200; thiazolidinediones's price starts at Rs 100 and goes up to Rs 500 for standard standalone doses.Also Read: How the weight loss market is prompting pharma biggies to look at India afreshInnovations in IndiaDrugmakers in India like Dr Reddy’s Laboratories has a combination of old and new products that include metformin and sulfonylurea, as well as SGLT2 inhibitors (oral medication that prevents SGLT2 protein from being absorbed by kidney) and semaglutides. MV Ramana, CEO, global generics, Dr Reddy’s Laboratories says the firm is actively evaluating multiple assets to ensure the right product-market fit and introduce to its portfolio.Deepak Arora, country lead-India and managing director, Sanofi India says that the country has evolved from being passive consumers of global technology to aggressive innovators. “Insulin delivery has shifted from thick needles to syringes and now to insulin pens. Capillary finger-strips have democratised basic diabetes management, making home testing a reality. The global standard has shifted towards continuous glucose monitoring [CGM] sensors that stream real-time data,” he says. Sanofi India, the domestic arm of the French drugmaker, made a reusable insulin pen AllStar in 2012. Arora says the firm’s diabetes product portfolio offers a range of legacy and new-age products.“Lantus and Apidra [basal insulin] represent our trusted legacy products. On the innovation front, we offer Toujeo, our second-generation basal insulin, alongside TouStar [a reusable insulin pen for Toujeo]; and Soliqua, a fixed-ratio combination therapy. We have engaged in strategic partnerships in oral anti-diabetic therapies, such as well-established brands like Amaryl and Cetapin,” he adds.Indian firms and startups are developing products such as insulin pumps and CGMs so that they don’t need to be imported. Ypsomed India, an Indian startup, has made low-cost insulin pens; others like Biocon and MJ Biopharm are trying to manufacture components of insulin pumps and CGMs at lower cost, while global medical equipment maker Abbott’s FreeStyle Libre (a popular CGM) is being assembled in India. Biocon’s interchangeable insulin glargine, developed alongside US-based Viatris in India and Malaysia, was the first interchangeable biosimilar approved by the US FDA in July 202; the company’s insulin glargine products are available in India.Also Read: India is an important partner for Novo’s R&D: Martin Holst LangeThe root problem, and is GLP-1 the solutionOne of the biggest reasons for the high incidences of diabetes in India is the carbohydrate-rich diet of most people, says Dr Jayakumar S, consultant-internal medicine and diabetologist, Magnet Hospital, Bengaluru. “The diet’s focus on protein and fibre is very low. Sedentary lifestyles, desk jobs and lower inclination towards physical activity contribute to it,” he adds.Biology and socio-economic factors are the other causes, says Venkataraman; South Asians are generally predisposed to developing diabetes at a younger age and lower BMI than the Western population. “We have greater visceral adiposity [excessive accumulation of fat deep inside the abdomen, which wraps around organs] and increased insulin resistance,” she says.The impact of GLP 1 drugs extends beyond diabetes, and is being recognized for their benefits to treat obesity, manage cardiovascular, renal, and metabolic conditions, which are common comorbidities among patients with type 2 diabetes. Venkataraman says the distinction between ‘diabetes drugs’ and ‘weight-loss drugs’ is becoming increasingly blurred because many of the newer therapies target the same underlying metabolic pathways, and that weight-loss drugs should not be interchangeably used for managing diabetes.

Ypsomed India, an Indian startup, has made low-cost insulin pens; others like Biocon and MJ Biopharm are trying to manufacture components of insulin pumps and CGMs at lower cost, while global medical equipment maker Abbott’s FreeStyle Libre (a popular CGM) is being assembled in India.

Biocon’s interchangeable insulin glargine, developed alongside US-based Viatris in India and Malaysia, was the first interchangeable biosimilar approved by the US FDA in July 202; the company’s insulin glargine products are available in India.
The root problem, and is GLP-1 the solution.

One of the biggest reasons for the high incidences of diabetes in India is the carbohydrate-rich diet of most people, says Dr Jayakumar S, consultant-internal medicine and diabetologist, Magnet Hospital, Bengaluru.
“The diet’s focus on protein and fibre is very low.
Sedentary lifestyles, desk jobs and lower inclination towards physical activity contribute to it,” he adds.
Biology and socio-economic factors are the other causes, says Venkataraman; South Asians are generally predisposed to developing diabetes at a younger age and lower BMI than the Western population.
“We have greater visceral adiposity [excessive accumulation of fat deep inside the abdomen, which wraps around organs] and increased insulin resistance,” she says.

The impact of GLP 1 drugs extends beyond diabetes, and is being recognized for their benefits to treat obesity, manage cardiovascular, renal, and metabolic conditions, which are common comorbidities among patients with type 2 diabetes.

Venkataraman says the distinction between ‘diabetes drugs’ and ‘weight-loss drugs’ is becoming increasingly blurred because many of the newer therapies target the same underlying metabolic pathways, and that weight-loss drugs should not be interchangeably used for managing diabetes.

Innovations in IndiaDrugmakers in India like Dr Reddy’s Laboratories has a combination of old and new products that include metformin and sulfonylurea, as well as SGLT2 inhibitors (oral medication that prevents SGLT2 protein from being absorbed by kidney) and semaglutides.

According to a study published in The Lancet Diabetes and Endocrinology journal, India is home to 90 million people living with diabetes, as of 2024 (the most recent year of study), and ranks second in the world, second to China, with 148 million diabetics.
